Dictators are most informativeThanks: Tuan Tran was supported by the Excellent Young Talents Program (Overseas) of the National Natural Science Foundation of China under Grant No. GG0010007003.

Vu Khac Ky Address: Department of Mathematics, FPT University, Hanoi, Vietnam Email address: kyvk2@fpt.edu.vn and Tuan Tran Address: School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Science and Technology of China, Anhui, China Email address: trantuan@ustc.edu.cn
Abstract.

We prove the Courtade–Kumar conjecture: among all Boolean functions f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f\colon\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}, a dictator retains the most information about a uniformly random input observed through independent binary noise.

1. Introduction

How much information about a noisy vector can be retained in one bit? Let XX be uniform on {−1,1}n\{-1,1\}^{n} and, for 0≤ρ≤10\leq\rho\leq 1, obtain YρY_{\rho} from XX by independently flipping each coordinate XiX_{i} with probability (1−ρ)/2(1-\rho)/2, so that larger ρ\rho means less noise. A one-bit summary of XX has the form f⁡(X)f(X) for a Boolean function f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}, and we seek a summary that shares as much information as possible with YρY_{\rho}. Courtade and Kumar [8] relate this question to the information bottleneck problem, where a compressed description should retain information about a correlated observation, and to the value of one bit of side information.

To measure the information preserved by a summary, recall that the Shannon entropy of a finite random variable UU with probability mass function pUp_{U} is H(U)=−∑upU(u)logpU(u)H(U)=-\sum_{u}p_{U}(u)\log p_{U}(u). We use natural logarithms and the convention 0​log⁡0=00\log 0=0. The conditional entropy H(U∣V)=∑v:pV​(v)>0pV(v)H(U∣V=v)H(U\mid V)=\sum_{v:p_{V}(v)>0}p_{V}(v)H(U\mid V=v) averages the entropy of the conditional distributions of UU given VV. The mutual information I⁡(U,V)=H⁡(U)−H⁡(U∣V)I(U;V)=H(U)-H(U\mid V) is therefore the average reduction in uncertainty about UU obtained by observing VV. Our objective is to maximize I⁡(f⁡(X),Yρ)I(f(X);Y_{\rho}) over all Boolean functions ff.

Kumar and Courtade conjectured in 2013 [18] that a single input coordinate is optimal, and studied the conjecture further in [8]. Such a summary, allowing a change of sign, is a signed dictator: f⁡(x)=σ​xif(x)=\sigma x_{i}, where 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n and σ∈{−1,1}\sigma\in\{-1,1\}, with random output σ​Xi\sigma X_{i}. To express its information value, write Hb​(p)=−p​log⁡p−(1−p)​log⁡(1−p)H_{\rm b}(p)=-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p) for binary entropy, and set

(1.1) H⁡(t)=Hb​((1−t)/2),Φ⁡(t)=log⁡2−H⁡(t).H(t)=H_{\rm b}((1-t)/2),\qquad\Phi(t)=\log 2-H(t).

Here H⁡(t)H(t) is the entropy of a sign-valued variable with mean tt. A Boolean function is called balanced when 𝔼​f=0\mathbb{E}f=0. Every signed dictator is balanced, with entropy log⁡2\log 2, and its conditional entropy given YρY_{\rho} is H⁡(ρ)H(\rho). Its mutual information is therefore Φ⁡(ρ)\Phi(\rho), which gives the benchmark in the following conjecture.

Conjecture 1.1 (Courtade–Kumar [18, 8]).

For every integer n≥1n\geq 1, every Boolean function f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}, and every ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1],

I⁡(f⁡(X),Yρ)≤Φ⁡(ρ).I(f(X);Y_{\rho})\leq\Phi(\rho).

The problem became a meeting point of information theory and Boolean analysis. Kindler, O’Donnell and Witmer [16] record the attention it attracted, while Yu and Tan’s 2022 monograph calls it “one of the most important open problems in information theory” [28, Section 9.1.2]. The latter places it alongside noise stability, noninteractive correlation distillation, and hypercontractivity.

The conjecture has led to sustained work on several related extremal problems. Anantharam, Gohari, Kamath and Nair [1] used hypercontractivity to study the weaker problem in which both vectors are reduced to Boolean outputs; Pichler, Piantanida and Matz [23] later proved this two-output inequality. Kindler, O’Donnell and Witmer [16] examined fixed-mean and continuous formulations, while Ordentlich, Shayevitz and Weinstein [22] improved the general upper bound by Fourier analysis. Samorodnitsky [24] established CK for 0≤ρ≤ρ00\leq\rho\leq\rho_{0}, with an absolute constant ρ0>0\rho_{0}>0. Yu [26, 27] subsequently strengthened this result in the balanced case to the explicit range 0≤ρ≤0.9140\leq\rho\leq 0.914, while also obtaining further bounds for arbitrary means.

A second line of work seeks a stronger functional inequality from which CK would follow. Anantharam, Bogdanov, Chakrabarti, Jayram and Nair [2] proposed a Hellinger-entropy strengthening and proved that it implies CK. Chen and Nair [4] placed these conjectures in an ordered family of Φ\Phi-entropy inequalities and related their small-noise limits to isoperimetry. Their introduction also records extensive work on the problem at a Simons workshop in 2015. Chen, Gohari and Nair [6] then developed a differential-equation approach and reduced a sufficient condition for balanced CK to four explicit inequalities. This program connects the conjecture to both functional inequalities and the evolution of entropy under noise. The ordering in [4] concerns the entropy parameter; it does not establish downward propagation in ρ\rho.

Li and Médard [20] studied noisy moments and noninteractive correlation distillation. Barnes and Özgür [3] proved an equivalence between balanced CK and a symmetrized Li–Médard conjecture. More recent work includes the coordinate-wise information bound of Javanmard and Woodruff [14]; its objective differs from information about the full noisy vector.

In this paper, we establish the Courtade–Kumar conjecture for every mean and correlation. Our proof uses log-Sobolev contraction [12], Harris association [13], and martingale entropy methods [9], with the Fourier normalization of O’Donnell [21].

Theorem 1.2.

The Courtade–Kumar conjecture holds.

The next result, proved in the companion paper [29], is a stability version of Theorem 1.2: if I⁡(f⁡(X),Yρ)I(f(X);Y_{\rho}) is close to Φ⁡(ρ)\Phi(\rho), then ff is close to a signed dictator.

Theorem 1.3 (Stability).

Let 0<ρ<10<\rho<1 and ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0. If f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} satisfies

I⁡(f⁡(X),Yρ)≥Φ⁡(ρ)−ε,I(f(X);Y_{\rho})\geq\Phi(\rho)-\varepsilon,

then there are 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n and σ∈{−1,1}\sigma\in\{-1,1\} such that

𝐏⁡(f⁡(X)≠σ​Xi)≤108​ερ2​(1−ρ)​H​(ρ).\mathbf{P}\big(f(X)\neq\sigma X_{i}\big)\leq\frac{10^{8}\,\varepsilon}{\rho^{2}(1-\rho)H(\rho)}.

Independent work. While preparing the present manuscript, we learned that Zijie Chen, Amin Gohari, Adel Javanmard, Honghao Lin, Vahab Mirrokni, Chandra Nair, and David P. Woodruff [5] had independently obtained a proof of the Courtade–Kumar conjecture. Their proof is substantially different from ours: their argument develops the differential-equation approach, whereas ours develops a new entropy-production and spectral framework. We thank them for their collegiality in coordinating the simultaneous posting of the two manuscripts on arXiv.

1.1. Methodology and relation to previous work

Our main technical contribution is a set of entropy-production and spectral estimates that control functions whose dependence is spread across many coordinates. These estimates retain both the contributions of selected coordinates and the variation outside them. Combined with local entropy comparisons near dictators, they give a bound valid across all noise levels, uniformly in the dimension. The key step is to make these two types of comparison meet without losing the information needed near the noiseless endpoint.

The difficulty at that endpoint is intrinsic to the problem. When ρ=1\rho=1, we have Y1=XY_{1}=X, so every balanced Boolean function carries the same information log⁡2\log 2. For example, parity on k≥2k\geq 2 coordinates carries Φ⁡(ρk)\Phi(\rho^{k}) information, which approaches the dictator value Φ⁡(ρ)\Phi(\rho) as ρ\rho tends to one, although its probability distance from every signed dictator remains 1/21/2. A qualitative proof must therefore resolve the sign of a vanishing deficit even for functions far from dictators. At the same time, higher Fourier levels become less strongly suppressed as the noise decreases, making estimates that discard their contribution insufficient.

Several ingredients come from earlier work. Samorodnitsky [24] proved CK at sufficiently high noise, and Yu [26, 27] substantially enlarged the known range for balanced functions. Yu’s Fourier bounds and local entropy comparisons provide important inputs to our argument. At low noise, Courtade and Kumar [8, Appendix B, Theorem 6] used edge isoperimetry to obtain dictator optimality in each fixed dimension. These endpoint results leave a dimension-independent comparison across all noise levels unresolved. We derive the needed forms of the local inputs to retain the dependence on the mean and to connect them to our spectral estimates.

Our estimates address this gap by comparing the rate at which noise creates conditional entropy with quadratic energy. Keeping track of where this energy lies allows us to distinguish dependence concentrated on one coordinate from dependence spread among several. We use the comparison in two complementary ways: integration gives an entropy bound in the intermediate range, while a differential argument rules out an excess over the dictator benchmark near the noiseless endpoint. Throughout, we retain the smaller initial entropy of an unbalanced bit, so the argument also covers arbitrary means.

Concavity and convexity reductions then turn the remaining comparisons into scalar inequalities independent of the dimension. This separates the analytic mechanism from the finite verification needed in the intermediate ranges; the final approach to the noiseless endpoint is analytic. Retaining quantitative margins in these comparisons leads to the stability theorem proved in the companion paper [29].

1.2. Outline of the proof

The proof compares the uncertainty left after observing the noisy vector with the uncertainty left by a dictator. For a fixed f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} with mean μ=𝔼​f\mu=\mathbb{E}f, write

(1.2) Aρ​(f)=I⁡(f⁡(X),Yρ),Eρ​(f)=H⁡(μ)−Aρ​(f).A_{\rho}(f)=I(f(X);Y_{\rho}),\qquad E_{\rho}(f)=H(\mu)-A_{\rho}(f).

Thus Eρ​(f)E_{\rho}(f) is the conditional entropy of the bit f⁡(X)f(X) given YρY_{\rho}. We must show that the gap

(1.3) Gf​(ρ)=Aρ​(f)−Φ⁡(ρ)=H⁡(ρ)−Eρ​(f)−Φ⁡(μ)G_{f}(\rho)=A_{\rho}(f)-\Phi(\rho)=H(\rho)-E_{\rho}(f)-\Phi(\mu)

is nonpositive. Keeping the term Φ⁡(μ)\Phi(\mu) is essential: the initial entropy of an unbalanced bit is smaller than that of a dictator.

A compression argument lets us assume that ff is increasing in each coordinate. We then distinguish functions close to a single coordinate from functions whose dependence is spread across several coordinates. For the first group, conditioning on one or two coordinates gives a direct entropy bound. For the second group, Fourier analysis measures how much dependence remains outside those coordinates.

To control the sources whose dependence is spread across coordinates, we study the rate of entropy change. Let Tρ​f​(y)=𝔼⁡[f⁡(X)∣Yρ=y]T_{\rho}f(y)=\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid Y_{\rho}=y] be the noise operator. Then Eρ​(f)=𝔼​H​(Tρ​f)E_{\rho}(f)=\mathbb{E}H(T_{\rho}f). Differentiating this expression reduces the problem to an inequality on each edge of the cube. The edge inequality gives a lower bound for the rate at which noise creates entropy, in terms of the current entropy and the coordinate influences of ff. Integrating that bound from the noiseless input gives a lower bound for Eρ​(f)E_{\rho}(f). Section 4 writes this integration as a change of variables; the resulting integral is called a profile clock there. The middle range is covered by the local bounds, this integrated entropy bound, and a direct Fourier-energy estimate.

At correlations close to one, the same comparison is used differentially. A stronger edge inequality, combined with the spectral comparison behind Theorem 6.5, controls Gf′​(ρ)G_{f}^{\prime}(\rho). If Gf​(ρ)>0G_{f}(\rho)>0, the bound makes this derivative nonnegative. Such a positive gap could not return to a nonpositive value at ρ=1\rho=1, where Gf​(1)=−Φ⁡(μ)≤0G_{f}(1)=-\Phi(\mu)\leq 0. The spectral estimate reaches the neighborhood already covered by the local entropy bound, so these two estimates account for every source. The source is held fixed throughout this differential argument.

The same scalar entropy profile supports both arguments. The decrease and log-concavity of v​H​(tanh⁡v)/tanh⁡vvH(\tanh v)/\tanh v (Lemma 4.1) let us replace a long list of influences by a few extremal values. They also allow an integrated entropy bound checked at one correlation to cover every larger correlation. A separate local bound propagates toward smaller correlations. These are monotonicity statements for the bounds used in the proof; they do not assert monotonicity of the conjecture itself.

These analytic reductions eliminate the dimension and the full list of influences, leaving explicit scalar inequalities. In the central range, affine interpolation reduces the scalar entropy bound to two noise endpoints, and a series argument controls the energy remainder throughout the interval. In the middle range, the integral is convex in the retained squared influences on each packing region (Lemmas 4.9 and 4.10), so its maximum occurs at a boundary value. Supporting lines then make each integral explicit, without certifying roots of the entropy profile. A fourth-moment inequality absorbs the mean correction in the two-coordinate region, so no mean partition remains. At high correlation, convexity reduces the compact certificate to four endpoint inequalities on each of 24 noise intervals. For atanh⁡ρ≥8\atanh\rho\geq 8, an explicit spectral choice and the local entropy comparison complete the proof analytically. The stronger marked-coordinate estimates needed for stability are developed in the companion paper [29]. The table summarizes the ranges covered by each argument. The remaining scalar checks are documented in Appendix A.

2. Preliminaries and monotone reduction

We begin with the representations of a Boolean function that will be used throughout the proof. Fourier coefficients describe its dependence on sets of coordinates, while the noise operator describes what an observer can infer about its value. The connection between these two descriptions lets us express conditional entropy and its rate of change in terms of the original function. We follow the uniform-cube conventions in [21, Chapters 1–2]; see also [11, Chapter IV] for the interpretation of the Fourier weights as an energy spectrum.

Unless another measure is specified, expectations use the uniform probability measure on {−1,1}n\{-1,1\}^{n}, and [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}. A Boolean function takes values in {−1,1}\{-1,1\}; when it is the input to the noise operator, we also call it the source. We allow real-valued functions in the definitions below, since conditional expectations of a Boolean function need not be Boolean.

2.1. Fourier–Walsh expansion and Fourier levels

For S⊆[n]S\subseteq[n], define the parity function χS​(x)=∏i∈Sxi\chi_{S}(x)=\prod_{i\in S}x_{i}, with χ∅=1\chi_{\varnothing}=1. If S≠TS\neq T, the product χS​χT\chi_{S}\chi_{T} contains a coordinate to an odd power, so independence and symmetry give 𝔼⁡[χS​χT]=0\mathbb{E}[\chi_{S}\chi_{T}]=0. Each parity has squared norm one. There are 2n2^{n} parities and the space of real functions on the cube has dimension 2n2^{n}, so they form an orthonormal basis for the inner product ⟨h,k⟩=𝔼⁡[h​k]\langle h,k\rangle=\mathbb{E}[hk]. Consequently every such function has a unique Fourier–Walsh expansion

h⁡(x)=∑S⊆[n]h^​(S)​χS​(x),h^​(S)=𝔼⁡[h⁡(X)​χS​(X)].h(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\widehat{h}(S)\chi_{S}(x),\qquad\widehat{h}(S)=\mathbb{E}[h(X)\chi_{S}(X)].

The coefficient at the empty set is the mean. A singleton coefficient, written h^​(i)=h^​({i})\widehat{h}(i)=\widehat{h}(\{i\}), measures correlation with one coordinate, while the coefficients with |S|=k|S|=k describe the degree-kk part of the multilinear expansion.

For a Boolean source ff, put μ=𝔼​f\mu=\mathbb{E}f. The Fourier weight at level kk is Wk​(f)=∑|S|=kf^​(S)2W_{k}(f)=\sum_{|S|=k}\widehat{f}(S)^{2}. Orthogonality gives Parseval’s identity

∑k=0nWk​(f)=𝔼​f2=1,W0​(f)=μ2,∑k≥1Wk​(f)=Var⁡(f)=1−μ2.\sum_{k=0}^{n}W_{k}(f)=\mathbb{E}f^{2}=1,\qquad W_{0}(f)=\mu^{2},\qquad\sum_{k\geq 1}W_{k}(f)=\Var(f)=1-\mu^{2}.

Thus these weights allocate the variance among Fourier degrees. For example, a dictator has all its weight at level one, whereas the parity of kk coordinates has all its weight at level kk. The weight W1W_{1} records the combined contribution of all coordinates, whereas distance to a dictator depends on the largest individual coefficient. Booleanity links these quantities when the low-degree weight is close to one: the Friedgut–Kalai–Naor theorem [10] says that a Boolean function with Fourier weight at most η\eta above level one is within C​ηC\eta in probability of a constant or a signed coordinate, for an absolute constant CC.

Write α⁡(f)=maxi⁡|f^​(i)|\alpha(f)=\max_{i}|\widehat{f}(i)|. For each sign σ\sigma, 𝔼⁡[f⁡(X)​σ​Xi]=1−2​𝐏​(f⁡(X)≠σ​Xi)\mathbb{E}[f(X)\sigma X_{i}]=1-2\mathbf{P}\big(f(X)\neq\sigma X_{i}\big), and therefore

(2.1) δ⁡(f):=mini∈[n],σ∈{−1,1}⁡𝐏⁡(f⁡(X)≠σ​Xi)=1−α⁡(f)2.\delta(f):=\min_{i\in[n],\,\sigma\in\{-1,1\}}\mathbf{P}\big(f(X)\neq\sigma X_{i}\big)=\frac{1-\alpha(f)}{2}.

This identity connects Fourier concentration with the distance used in the stability theorem. We omit the argument ff when the source is fixed and order coordinates by decreasing |f^​(i)||\widehat{f}(i)|. When two coordinates are needed and n=1n=1, we append an unused coordinate; this changes neither entropy nor Fourier weights.

2.2. Noise, posterior means, and information

The noise operator averages a function over independent perturbations of its input. If Zi=yiZ_{i}=y_{i} with probability (1+ρ)/2(1+\rho)/2 and Zi=−yiZ_{i}=-y_{i} otherwise, independently over ii, then Tρ​h​(y)=𝔼⁡[h⁡(Z)]T_{\rho}h(y)=\mathbb{E}[h(Z)]. The joint distribution of XX and YρY_{\rho} is symmetric in its two arguments, so the same formula gives Tρ​h​(y)=𝔼⁡[h⁡(X)∣Yρ=y]T_{\rho}h(y)=\mathbb{E}[h(X)\mid Y_{\rho}=y]. Independence gives 𝔼⁡[χS​(Z)]=ρ|S|​χS​(y)\mathbb{E}[\chi_{S}(Z)]=\rho^{|S|}\chi_{S}(y), hence

Tρ​h=∑Sρ|S|​h^​(S)​χS,Tη​Tρ=Tη​ρ.T_{\rho}h=\sum_{S}\rho^{|S|}\widehat{h}(S)\chi_{S},\qquad T_{\eta}T_{\rho}=T_{\eta\rho}.

In particular, noise preserves the mean and attenuates each Fourier degree separately. The second identity expresses the effect of applying two successive rounds of noise; it follows by multiplying their factors on every parity. For a Boolean source, Parseval now gives

Var⁡(Tρ​f)=∑k≥1ρ2​k​Wk​(f).\Var(T_{\rho}f)=\sum_{k\geq 1}\rho^{2k}W_{k}(f).

This formula explains why low-degree information is especially useful at small correlation, and why discarding higher levels costs more as ρ\rho approaches one.

Set gρ=Tρ​fg_{\rho}=T_{\rho}f. Since a sign-valued random variable is determined in distribution by its mean, 𝐏⁡{f⁡(X)=1∣Yρ=y}=(1+gρ​(y))/2\mathbf{P}\{f(X)=1\mid Y_{\rho}=y\}=(1+g_{\rho}(y))/2. Thus gρg_{\rho} records the observer’s posterior bias: values near zero mean substantial uncertainty, while values near ±1\pm 1 mean that the bit can be predicted with high confidence. By symmetry of the entropy function in (1.1), the posterior entropy at yy is H​(gρ​(y))H(g_{\rho}(y)). Thus the quantities in (1.2) can be written as

(2.2) Eρ​(f)=𝔼​H​(gρ),Aρ​(f)=H⁡(μ)−Eρ​(f)=𝔼​Φ​(gρ)−Φ⁡(μ).E_{\rho}(f)=\mathbb{E}H(g_{\rho}),\qquad A_{\rho}(f)=H(\mu)-E_{\rho}(f)=\mathbb{E}\Phi(g_{\rho})-\Phi(\mu).

The source is balanced when μ=0\mu=0. Its initial entropy is then log⁡2\log 2; an unbalanced source starts with less entropy, which is why the term Φ⁡(μ)\Phi(\mu) must be retained in comparisons with dictators. Constant sources have zero information and can always be treated directly.

We use the signed gap GfG_{f} from (1.3) for the extremal argument and the deficit Δρ​(f)=−Gf​(ρ)\Delta_{\rho}(f)=-G_{f}(\rho) for stability. Both measure the same comparison, with opposite sign. For a dictator, gρ​(y)=±ρ​yig_{\rho}(y)=\pm\rho y_{i}, so Eρ​(f)=H​(ρ)E_{\rho}(f)=H(\rho) and Aρ​(f)=Φ​(ρ)A_{\rho}(f)=\Phi(\rho), confirming the benchmark. The entropy function is even and concave, decreases on [0,1][0,1], and satisfies H′​(t)=−atanh⁡tH^{\prime}(t)=-\atanh t on (−1,1)(-1,1).

2.3. Monotone compression and influences

An increasing, or monotone, Boolean function satisfies f⁡(x)≤f⁡(y)f(x)\leq f(y) whenever xi≤yix_{i}\leq y_{i} for every coordinate. To reduce to this case, we sort the two values of ff along each coordinate fiber, placing the smaller value at −1-1 and the larger at 11. The next lemma shows that this preserves the mean and can only increase information, so an upper bound for increasing sources suffices for every source. This qualitative reduction is due to Courtade and Kumar [8, Lemma 2 and Remark 2]. Li and Médard [20, Theorem 3.2] state the corresponding result for every convex function of the noisy output. We include the short proof because the sorting step explains how the arbitrary-mean problem reduces to increasing sources.

Lemma 2.1 (Coordinate compression [8]).

Every f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} admits an increasing g:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}g:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} with 𝔼​g=𝔼​f\mathbb{E}g=\mathbb{E}f such that

Aρ​(g)≥Aρ​(f)for every ​ρ∈[0,1],g^​(i)≥|f^​(i)|for every ​i∈[n].A_{\rho}(g)\geq A_{\rho}(f)\quad\text{for every }\rho\in[0,1],\qquad\widehat{g}(i)\geq|\widehat{f}(i)|\quad\text{for every }i\in[n].

In particular, δ⁡(g)≤δ⁡(f)\delta(g)\leq\delta(f).

Proof.

Write f⁡(xi,z)=u⁡(z)+xi​v​(z)f(x_{i},z)=u(z)+x_{i}v(z). Sorting the two values on each ii-fiber replaces vv by |v||v| and preserves the mean. For a fixed outside output yy, put b=Tρ​u​(y)b=T_{\rho}u(y), d=Tρ​v​(y)d=T_{\rho}v(y), and e=Tρ​|v|​(y)e=T_{\rho}|v|(y), where the noise operator acts on the remaining coordinates. Positivity gives |d|≤e|d|\leq e. By convexity of Φ\Phi, the function Φ⁡(b+t)+Φ⁡(b−t)2\frac{\Phi(b+t)+\Phi(b-t)}{2} is even and nondecreasing for t≥0t\geq 0 on its domain. Its value at ρ​d\rho d is therefore at most its value at ρ​e\rho e. Averaging shows that sorting does not decrease AρA_{\rho}.

The sorted sections are the pointwise minimum and maximum of the original sections, so sorting preserves monotonicity in previously sorted coordinates. Sorting each coordinate once therefore produces an increasing gg, and the same construction works for every ρ∈[0,1]\rho\in[0,1].

Sorting any coordinate other than ii preserves the iith singleton coefficient, while sorting ii replaces 𝔼​v\mathbb{E}v by 𝔼​|v|≥|𝔼​v|\mathbb{E}|v|\geq|\mathbb{E}v|. This proves the coefficient comparison and hence the assertion about δ\delta. ∎

We keep this compressed source fixed in each differential argument, so its Fourier coefficients are constants as ρ\rho varies. Monotonicity also makes the singleton coefficients especially useful, because they equal coordinate influences, as we now explain.

Let x⊕ix^{\oplus i} denote xx with coordinate ii flipped. The influence of ii on a Boolean function is

Infi⁡(f)=𝐏⁡(f⁡(X)≠f⁡(X⊕i)).\operatorname{Inf}_{i}(f)=\mathbf{P}\big(f(X)\neq f(X^{\oplus i})\big).

For a real-valued function hh, its discrete derivative is the half difference between the two values on an ii-fiber:

∂ih⁡(x−i)=h⁡(x−i,1)−h⁡(x−i,−1)2.\partial_{i}h(x_{-i})=\frac{h(x_{-i},1)-h(x_{-i},-1)}{2}.

For Boolean ff, this derivative lies in {−1,0,1}\{-1,0,1\}, and its absolute value indicates whether flipping ii changes the output. Therefore Infi⁡(f)=𝔼​|∂if|=𝔼​(∂if)2\operatorname{Inf}_{i}(f)=\mathbb{E}|\partial_{i}f|=\mathbb{E}(\partial_{i}f)^{2}. For increasing ff the derivative is nonnegative, giving Infi⁡(f)=𝔼​∂if=f^​(i)\operatorname{Inf}_{i}(f)=\mathbb{E}\partial_{i}f=\widehat{f}(i). In particular some singleton coefficient is positive for every nonconstant increasing source. This identification allows the edge estimates below to retain information about individual coordinates of the original function.

Two distinct coordinates also satisfy

(2.3) f^​(i)+f^​(j)=𝔼⁡[f⁡(X)​(Xi+Xj)]≤𝔼​|Xi+Xj|=1(i≠j).\widehat{f}(i)+\widehat{f}(j)=\mathbb{E}[f(X)(X_{i}+X_{j})]\leq\mathbb{E}|X_{i}+X_{j}|=1\qquad(i\neq j).

For the ordered nonnegative coefficients of an increasing source, this implies f^​(2)≤1/2\widehat{f}(2)\leq 1/2. We will use such constraints when deciding which coordinates to retain in an entropy estimate.

2.4. The Laplacian and entropy production

To study how entropy changes with the amount of noise, we use the cube Laplacian. Its coordinate part is ℒi​h​(x)=[h⁡(x)−h⁡(x⊕i)]/2=xi​∂ih⁡(x−i)\mathcal{L}_{i}h(x)=[h(x)-h(x^{\oplus i})]/2=x_{i}\partial_{i}h(x_{-i}), and ℒ=∑iℒi\mathcal{L}=\sum_{i}\mathcal{L}_{i}. Thus ℒi\mathcal{L}_{i} retains precisely the Fourier terms containing ii, while ℒ​χS=|S|​χS\mathcal{L}\chi_{S}=|S|\chi_{S}. The associated Dirichlet energy has both an edge and a Fourier form:

(2.4) Dir⁡(h)=𝔼⁡[h​ℒ​h]=∑i𝔼​(∂ih)2=∑S|S|​h^​(S)2.\operatorname{Dir}(h)=\mathbb{E}[h\mathcal{L}h]=\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}(\partial_{i}h)^{2}=\sum_{S}|S|\widehat{h}(S)^{2}.

It measures variation across cube edges, assigning a Fourier mode one unit of energy for each coordinate it uses. For Boolean ff it is the total influence ∑iInfi⁡(f)\sum_{i}\operatorname{Inf}_{i}(f). We write Diri⁡(h)=𝔼⁡[h​ℒi​h]\operatorname{Dir}_{i}(h)=\mathbb{E}[h\mathcal{L}_{i}h] and DirK⁡(h)=∑i∈KDiri⁡(h)\operatorname{Dir}_{K}(h)=\sum_{i\in K}\operatorname{Dir}_{i}(h).

Entropy has a corresponding nonlinear energy. For |g|<1|g|<1, define

(2.5) 𝒟i​(g)=𝔼⁡[(ℒi​g)​atanh⁡g],D⁡(g)=∑i𝒟i​(g).\mathcal{D}_{i}(g)=\mathbb{E}[(\mathcal{L}_{i}g)\atanh g],\qquad D(g)=\sum_{i}\mathcal{D}_{i}(g).

On a fiber with values g+,g−g_{+},g_{-}, its contribution is (g+−g−)​(atanh⁡g+−atanh⁡g−)/4(g_{+}-g_{-})(\atanh g_{+}-\atanh g_{-})/4, which is nonnegative because atanh\atanh is increasing. These quantities are therefore suited to measuring entropy production. For a nonconstant Boolean source and 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, the strictly positive noise kernel gives |Tρ​f|<1|T_{\rho}f|<1, so all these expressions and derivatives are finite.

Fourier differentiation gives ρ​∂ρTρ​f=ℒ​Tρ​f\rho\partial_{\rho}T_{\rho}f=\mathcal{L}T_{\rho}f. Combining it with H′=−atanhH^{\prime}=-\atanh yields

(2.6) −ρ​Eρ′​(f)=D⁡(Tρ​f),ρ​Gf′​(ρ)=D⁡(Tρ​f)−ρ​atanh⁡ρ.-\rho E^{\prime}_{\rho}(f)=D(T_{\rho}f),\qquad\rho G_{f}^{\prime}(\rho)=D(T_{\rho}f)-\rho\atanh\rho.

Equivalently, in noise time τ=−log⁡ρ\tau=-\log\rho, the operator is Te−τ=e−τ​ℒT_{e^{-\tau}}=e^{-\tau\mathcal{L}} and d​Ee−τ​(f)/d​τ=D⁡(Te−τ​f)dE_{e^{-\tau}}(f)/d\tau=D(T_{e^{-\tau}}f). Increasing τ\tau adds noise and creates conditional entropy. The dictator has production ρ​atanh⁡ρ\rho\atanh\rho, so the second identity turns an entropy-production comparison into control of the slope of the information gap. We often write u=atanh⁡ρu=\atanh\rho; this parameter tends to infinity at the noiseless endpoint.

The differential argument uses the following elementary principle. A positive gap cannot return to a nonpositive endpoint value if its slope is nonnegative whenever the gap is positive.

Lemma 2.2.

Let G:[a,b]→ℝG:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R} be continuous, differentiable on (a,b)(a,b), and G⁡(b)≤0G(b)\leq 0. If G′​(x)≥0G^{\prime}(x)\geq 0 whenever G⁡(x)>0G(x)>0, then G≤0G\leq 0 on [a,b][a,b].

Proof.

If a positive component exists, GG is nondecreasing on that component, whereas its right endpoint has value zero (or at most zero if the endpoint is bb). This is impossible. Continuity covers the left endpoint. ∎

At the endpoints, Gf​(0)=0G_{f}(0)=0 and Gf​(1)=−Φ⁡(μ)≤0G_{f}(1)=-\Phi(\mu)\leq 0. For interior correlations, a hypothetical positive gap gives Eρ​(f)<H⁡(ρ)−Φ⁡(μ)≤H⁡(ρ)E_{\rho}(f)<H(\rho)-\Phi(\mu)\leq H(\rho). We also use the scalar expansion

(2.7) Φ⁡(t)=∑k≥1t2​k2​k​(2​k−1),t22≤Φ⁡(t)≤(log⁡2)​t2.\Phi(t)=\sum_{k\geq 1}\frac{t^{2k}}{2k(2k-1)},\qquad\frac{t^{2}}{2}\leq\Phi(t)\leq(\log 2)t^{2}.

Indeed, differentiating the series gives atanh⁡t\atanh t, and the value at zero fixes the integration constant; continuity covers |t|=1|t|=1. It follows in particular that a positive gap requires |μ|<2​H​(ρ)|\mu|<\sqrt{2H(\rho)}. Thus sources that could violate the bound at very large correlation must have small mean. When applying Lemma 2.2, we hold this source fixed on each positive component. Auxiliary projections and scalar parameters may depend on ρ\rho, but their derivatives do not enter the argument.

2.5. Finite reversible Markov semigroups

The continuous noise parameter has a similar meaning on a general finite state space. We explain this setting because the entropy inequalities in Section 6.3 use only reversibility and spectral decomposition. For background on transition matrices, reversibility, and continuous-time chains, see [19, Chapters 1, 12, and 20].

Let Ω\Omega be a finite set and let ν⁡(x)>0\nu(x)>0 for x∈Ωx\in\Omega, with ∑xν⁡(x)=1\sum_{x}\nu(x)=1. A transition matrix ps​(x,y)p_{s}(x,y) records the probability of moving from xx to yy in time s≥0s\geq 0; its entries are nonnegative and each row sums to one. It acts on a function by averaging over the possible destinations:

Ps​h​(x)=∑y∈Ωps​(x,y)​h​(y)=𝔼⁡[h⁡(Zs)∣Z0=x].P_{s}h(x)=\sum_{y\in\Omega}p_{s}(x,y)h(y)=\mathbb{E}[h(Z_{s})\mid Z_{0}=x].

Here (Zs)s≥0(Z_{s})_{s\geq 0} is the corresponding continuous-time Markov chain. The family (Ps)s≥0(P_{s})_{s\geq 0} is a Markov semigroup when it is continuous in ss, P0=IP_{0}=I, and Ps+t=Ps​PtP_{s+t}=P_{s}P_{t}. The last identity says that running the chain for time ss and then for time tt has the same effect as running it for time s+ts+t. In particular, these operators preserve constants and positivity.

The measure ν\nu is stationary if ∑xν⁡(x)​ps​(x,y)=ν⁡(y)\sum_{x}\nu(x)p_{s}(x,y)=\nu(y): starting the chain with distribution ν\nu leaves its distribution unchanged. It is reversible with respect to ν\nu if ν⁡(x)​ps​(x,y)=ν⁡(y)​ps​(y,x)\nu(x)p_{s}(x,y)=\nu(y)p_{s}(y,x) for every s,x,ys,x,y. This detailed-balance identity implies stationarity and says that PsP_{s} is self-adjoint for ⟨h,k⟩ν=𝔼ν​[h​k]\langle h,k\rangle_{\nu}=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[hk], where 𝔼ν​h=∑xν⁡(x)​h​(x)\mathbb{E}_{\nu}h=\sum_{x}\nu(x)h(x).

In finite dimension we can write Ps=e−s​ℒP_{s}=e^{-s\mathcal{L}}. Our sign convention makes ℒ\mathcal{L} nonnegative; the usual Markov generator is −ℒ-\mathcal{L}. If q⁡(x,y)≥0q(x,y)\geq 0 is the rate of jumping from xx to y≠xy\neq x, then

ℒ​h​(x)=∑y≠xq⁡(x,y)​[h⁡(x)−h⁡(y)],ν⁡(x)​q​(x,y)=ν⁡(y)​q​(y,x).\mathcal{L}h(x)=\sum_{y\neq x}q(x,y)[h(x)-h(y)],\qquad\nu(x)q(x,y)=\nu(y)q(y,x).

Pairing the terms for (x,y)(x,y) and (y,x)(y,x) gives

⟨h,ℒ​k⟩ν=12​∑x≠yν⁡(x)​q​(x,y)​[h⁡(x)−h⁡(y)]​[k⁡(x)−k⁡(y)].\langle h,\mathcal{L}k\rangle_{\nu}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x\neq y}\nu(x)q(x,y)[h(x)-h(y)][k(x)-k(y)].

Taking k=hk=h shows that Dir⁡(h)=⟨h,ℒ​h⟩ν≥0\operatorname{Dir}(h)=\langle h,\mathcal{L}h\rangle_{\nu}\geq 0. Reversibility therefore gives an orthonormal eigenbasis with eigenvalues λ≥0\lambda\geq 0. If hλh_{\lambda} denotes the projection of hh onto an eigenspace, then Ps​h=∑λe−s​λ​hλP_{s}h=\sum_{\lambda}e^{-s\lambda}h_{\lambda} and Dir⁡(h)=∑λλ​‖hλ‖2,ν2\operatorname{Dir}(h)=\sum_{\lambda}\lambda\|h_{\lambda}\|_{2,\nu}^{2}. These are the general counterparts of Fourier attenuation and Fourier energy on the cube.

For the cube, take uniform ν\nu and let each coordinate flip independently at rate 1/21/2. This gives the Laplacian defined above and Ps=Te−sP_{s}=T_{e^{-s}}, so s=log⁡(1/ρ)s=\log(1/\rho). The Walsh characters are its eigenfunctions, with eigenvalues |S||S|. In the general statements, Dir\operatorname{Dir} and D⁡(h)=𝔼ν​[(ℒ​h)​atanh⁡h]D(h)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[(\mathcal{L}h)\atanh h] use the same definitions with the specified stationary measure. No irreducibility assumption is needed for those statements.

3. Local entropy and Fourier bounds at low correlation

We prove CK through correlation 0.9140.914 while developing the local estimates used in the rest of the paper. The balanced conclusion on this range is due to Yu [27]; the purpose here is to keep the mean and the quantitative slack visible in a form compatible with the later argument. We first retain one or two coordinates, apply noise on them exactly, and bound the remaining noise by entropy contraction. For sources without a dominant coordinate, an odd lift allows Yu’s first-level bound and a Khintchine-type estimate to control the mean together with the level-one weight. A quadratic entropy bound then completes the interval, with margins that also imply stability.

3.1. Entropy contraction

Entropy contraction quantifies how averaging reduces a function’s departure from its mean. For a nonnegative function vv, write Ent⁡(v)=𝔼⁡[v​log⁡v]−𝔼​v​log⁡𝔼​v\Ent(v)=\mathbb{E}[v\log v]-\mathbb{E}v\log\mathbb{E}v; if 𝔼​v=1\mathbb{E}v=1, this is the relative entropy of the probability density vv with respect to the uniform measure. Applying it to 1+g1+g and 1−g1-g converts this functional inequality into a statement about the conditional entropy of a bit. We first collect the cube inequalities (see [21, Sections 2.3, 9.3, and Exercises 10.23–10.24]) needed for that conversion and for the later influence estimate, using ‖h‖p=(𝔼​|h|p)1/p\|h\|_{p}=(\mathbb{E}|h|^{p})^{1/p}.

Theorem 3.1 (Cube functional inequalities [12, 21]).

For every h:{−1,1}n→ℝh:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}, with the uniform measure, Var⁡(h)≤Dir⁡(h)\Var(h)\leq\operatorname{Dir}(h) and Ent⁡(h2)≤2​Dir⁡(h)\Ent(h^{2})\leq 2\operatorname{Dir}(h). For 0≤η≤10\leq\eta\leq 1, hypercontractivity gives ‖Tη​h‖2≤‖h‖1+η2\|T_{\eta}h\|_{2}\leq\|h\|_{1+\eta^{2}}.

The following standard consequence of the cube log-Sobolev inequality is stated in our normalization; see [12] and [21, Exercise 10.23].

Lemma 3.2 (Entropy contraction).

For f:{−1,1}n→[0,∞)f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to[0,\infty), write Ent⁡(f)=𝔼⁡[f​log⁡f]−𝔼​f​log⁡𝔼​f\Ent(f)=\mathbb{E}[f\log f]-\mathbb{E}f\log\mathbb{E}f. For 0≤η≤10\leq\eta\leq 1, Ent⁡(Tη​f)≤η2​Ent⁡(f)\Ent(T_{\eta}f)\leq\eta^{2}\Ent(f). Consequently, for every g:{−1,1}n→[−1,1]g:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to[-1,1],

𝔼​H​(Tη​g)≥η2​𝔼​H​(g)+(1−η2)​H​(𝔼​g).\mathbb{E}H(T_{\eta}g)\geq\eta^{2}\mathbb{E}H(g)+(1-\eta^{2})H(\mathbb{E}g).
Proof.

Entropy tensorizes: Ent⁡(f)≤∑i𝔼​Enti⁡(f)\Ent(f)\leq\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}\Ent_{i}(f), where Enti\Ent_{i} denotes entropy on the iith coordinate with the other coordinates fixed. This follows inductively from the entropy chain rule and convexity of f↦Ent⁡(f)f\mapsto\Ent(f). For f>0f>0, convexity follows from the second variation 𝔼⁡[z2/f]−(𝔼​z)2/𝔼​f≥0\mathbb{E}[z^{2}/f]-(\mathbb{E}z)^{2}/\mathbb{E}f\geq 0, by Cauchy–Schwarz.

On a two-point fiber write f±=m⁡(1±t)f_{\pm}=m(1\pm t). Its entropy is m​Φ​(t)m\Phi(t) and its entropy Dirichlet form is m​t​atanh⁡tmt\atanh t. The power series of Φ\Phi and atanh\atanh give t​atanh⁡t≥2​Φ​(t)t\atanh t\geq 2\Phi(t) for |t|<1|t|<1. Now set fτ=Te−τ​ff_{\tau}=T_{e^{-\tau}}f. Integration by parts on the cube yields

−dd​τ​Ent⁡(fτ)=∑i𝔼⁡[ℒi​fτ​ℒi​log⁡fτ]≥2​∑i𝔼​Enti⁡(fτ)≥2​Ent⁡(fτ),-\frac{d}{d\tau}\Ent(f_{\tau})=\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}_{i}f_{\tau}\,\mathcal{L}_{i}\log f_{\tau}]\geq 2\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}\Ent_{i}(f_{\tau})\geq 2\Ent(f_{\tau}),

Integration proves the contraction inequality. Nonnegative ff is treated by applying the result to f+ϵf+\epsilon and taking ϵ↓0\epsilon\downarrow 0; the cases η=0,1\eta=0,1 follow by continuity.

Finally, apply the contraction inequality to 1+g1+g and 1−g1-g and use Ent⁡(1+g)+Ent⁡(1−g)=2​{H⁡(𝔼​g)−𝔼​H​(g)}\Ent(1+g)+\Ent(1-g)=2\{H(\mathbb{E}g)-\mathbb{E}H(g)\}. This gives the posterior-entropy bound. ∎

Let TηKT_{\eta}^{K} denote noise applied only to coordinates in a fixed core KK, and define fK:{−1,1}K→[−1,1]f_{K}:\{-1,1\}^{K}\to[-1,1] by fK=𝔼⁡[f∣XK]f_{K}=\mathbb{E}[f\mid X_{K}]. (3.1) Eη​(f)≥η2​𝔼​H​(TηK​f)+(1−η2)​𝔼XK​H​(TηK​fK).E_{\eta}(f)\geq\eta^{2}\mathbb{E}H(T_{\eta}^{K}f)+(1-\eta^{2})\mathbb{E}_{X_{K}}H(T_{\eta}^{K}f_{K}).

This also holds when the outside cube is a singleton.

Corollary 3.3.

For every f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} and 0≤η,ρ0≤10\leq\eta,\rho_{0}\leq 1, Aη​ρ0​(f)≤η2​Aρ0​(f)A_{\eta\rho_{0}}(f)\leq\eta^{2}A_{\rho_{0}}(f). In particular, Aρ​(f)≤ρ2​H​(μ)A_{\rho}(f)\leq\rho^{2}H(\mu). If |μ|≥61/100|\mu|\geq 61/100, the CK inequality holds at every correlation.

Proof.

For g:{−1,1}n→[−1,1]g:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to[-1,1] with 𝔼​g=μ\mathbb{E}g=\mu, 12​[Ent⁡(1+g)+Ent⁡(1−g)]=𝔼​Φ​(g)−Φ⁡(μ)\tfrac{1}{2}[\Ent(1+g)+\Ent(1-g)]=\mathbb{E}\Phi(g)-\Phi(\mu). Apply Lemma 3.2 to 1±Tρ0​f1\pm T_{\rho_{0}}f and use the semigroup property. Taking ρ0=1\rho_{0}=1 gives the second inequality. The entropy series and log⁡2<347/500\log 2<347/500 give H⁡(61/100)<347/500−(61/100)2/2−(61/100)4/12<1/2H(61/100)<347/500-(61/100)^{2}/2-(61/100)^{4}/12<1/2; now use Φ⁡(ρ)≥ρ2/2\Phi(\rho)\geq\rho^{2}/2. ∎

This is how the estimate at ρ=3/5\rho=3/5 will cover the interval down to zero.

3.2. An exact one-coordinate inequality at arbitrary mean

The balanced specialization of the next estimate is Yu’s one-coordinate bound [27, Theorem 4.6 and Remark 4.7]. His Section 6 gives a broader framework for arbitrary means. We give the direct entropy-contraction proof of the form needed here, including the convex mean correction that permits comparison with a dictator. For 0≤a≤10\leq a\leq 1, define

(3.2) Mρ​(a)=(1−ρ2)​H​(ρ​a)−(1−ρ2​a)​H​(ρ).M_{\rho}(a)=(1-\rho^{2})H(\rho a)-(1-\rho^{2}a)H(\rho).

This is the lower bound for the information deficit obtained by retaining a coefficient of magnitude aa. Its value is zero at a=1a=1, and concavity will allow one verified value to control an entire neighborhood of the dictators.

Theorem 3.4 (Local entropy comparison).

Let f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}, i∈[n]i\in[n], and 0≤ρ≤10\leq\rho\leq 1. Then

Eρ​(f)≥1−ρ22​[H⁡(μ+ρ​f^​(i))+H⁡(μ−ρ​f^​(i))]+ρ2​|f^​(i)|​H​(ρ).E_{\rho}(f)\geq\frac{1-\rho^{2}}{2}\bigl[H(\mu+\rho\widehat{f}(i))+H(\mu-\rho\widehat{f}(i))\bigr]+\rho^{2}|\widehat{f}(i)|H(\rho).

Bρ,a​(μ)=Φ⁡(μ)+(1−ρ2)​{H⁡(μ+ρ​a)+H⁡(μ−ρ​a)2−H⁡(ρ​a)}.B_{\rho,a}(\mu)=\Phi(\mu)+(1-{\rho^{2}})\left\{\frac{H(\mu+\rho a)+H(\mu-\rho a)}{2}-H(\rho a)\right\}.

−H′′​(μ+ρ​a)+H′′​(μ−ρ​a)2=12​∑σ∈{−1,1}1−σ​μ(1−σ​μ)2−ρ2​a2≤1(1−ρ2)​(1−μ2).-\frac{H^{\prime\prime}(\mu+\rho a)+H^{\prime\prime}(\mu-\rho a)}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\sigma\in\{-1,1\}}\frac{1-\sigma\mu}{(1-\sigma\mu)^{2}-\rho^{2}a^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{(1-\rho^{2})(1-\mu^{2})}.

Each denominator is bounded below by (1−ρ2)​(1−σ​μ)2(1-\rho^{2})(1-\sigma\mu)^{2}. It follows that B′′​(μ)≥0B^{\prime\prime}(\mu)\geq 0, so evenness and B⁡(0)=0B(0)=0 give B≥0B\geq 0. Finally Mρ′′(a)=−(1−ρ2)ρ2/(1−ρ2a2)<0M^{\prime\prime}_{\rho}(a)=-(1-{\rho^{2}}){\rho^{2}}/(1-{\rho^{2}}a^{2})<0, proving the last claim. ∎

Lemma 3.5.

For fixed a∈[0,1]a\in[0,1], if Mρ0​(a)≥0M_{\rho_{0}}(a)\geq 0 at some 0<ρ0<10<\rho_{0}<1, then

Mρ​(a)ρ2≥Mρ0​(a)ρ02≥0(0<ρ≤ρ0).\frac{M_{\rho}(a)}{\rho^{2}}\geq\frac{M_{\rho_{0}}(a)}{\rho_{0}^{2}}\geq 0\qquad(0<\rho\leq\rho_{0}).

Suppose first that 0<a<10<a<1, and set F⁡(ρ)=Mρ​(a)/ρ2F(\rho)=M_{\rho}(a)/\rho^{2}. With cn=1/[2​n​(2​n−1)]c_{n}=1/[2n(2n-1)], the entropy series gives

The coefficient sign is determined by the ratio of its two positive terms. With b⁡(x)=x/(1−ax)b(x)=x/(1-a^{x}), that ratio is

The derivative series has the same sign pattern. If every coefficient is nonnegative, then FF increases strictly. Otherwise let mm be the last index with dm<0d_{m}<0. 4. Scalar entropy inequalities and profile clocks

The low-correlation argument retained total Fourier weights. We now keep the individual singleton coefficients, which record how the first-level dependence is distributed among coordinates. The bridge to entropy is an inequality on one edge: its production can be bounded below using only its average entropy and the half difference of its endpoint values. We encode that bound in a scalar function Be​(q)B_{e}(q). Convexity will allow us to average edges in each coordinate direction, and then to integrate the resulting production bound.

4.1. The scalar entropy profile

Consider first an edge with posterior values −t,t-t,t, where 0<t<10<t<1. Its average entropy is H⁡(t)H(t), its half difference is tt, and its entropy production is t​atanh⁡tt\atanh t. Writing v=atanh⁡tv=\atanh t, we denote the ratio of entropy to edge size by F⁡(v)F(v) and use its inverse to define the production profile: for v,e,q>0v,e,q>0, put

(4.1) F⁡(v)=H⁡(tanh⁡v)tanh⁡v,Be​(q)=q​F−1​(e/q).F(v)=\frac{H(\tanh v)}{\tanh v},\qquad B_{e}(q)=qF^{-1}(e/q).

The next lemma shows that FF decreases bijectively from (0,∞)(0,\infty) onto (0,∞)(0,\infty), so the inverse is well defined. Equivalently, choose the unique t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1) satisfying e​t=q​H​(t)et=qH(t) and set Be​(q)=q​atanh⁡tB_{e}(q)=q\atanh t, with Be​(0)=0B_{e}(0)=0 by continuity. For an actual centered edge this recovers its production exactly; Lemma 4.4 proves that it is a lower bound for every edge with the prescribed entropy and half difference. The convexity properties established first are what allow that pointwise inequality to survive averaging.

4.3. Integrating from the Boolean endpoint

The production bound can be integrated because the original source has zero conditional entropy at ρ=1\rho=1. Use noise time τ=−log⁡ρ\tau=-\log\rho and rescale entropy as y=Eρ​(f)/ρy=E_{\rho}(f)/\rho. The scaling identity for BB will give a differential inequality of the form d​y/d​τ≥y+Pf​(y)dy/d\tau\geq y+P_{f}(y), where the function PfP_{f} depends only on the source’s singleton coefficients. Separation of variables then leads to the integral below, called a profile clock: it measures the time in the scalar comparison equation needed to reach entropy level yy.

Define the singleton profile and its clock by

(4.4) Pf​(y)=∑iBy​(|f^​(i)|),TPf​(v)=∫0vd​yy+Pf​(y).P_{f}(y)=\sum_{i}B_{y}(|\widehat{f}(i)|),\qquad T_{P_{f}}(v)=\int_{0}^{v}\frac{dy}{y+P_{f}(y)}.

The condition W1>0W_{1}>0 makes this integral finite near zero and holds for every nonconstant increasing source. A dictator has one singleton coefficient of magnitude one, so its profile is simply By​(1)B_{y}(1); this gives the reference clock for the comparisons below.

Theorem 4.5 (Profile clock).

If f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} and W1​(f)>0W_{1}(f)>0, then for 0<ρ<10<\rho<1,

TPf​(Eρ​(f)/ρ)≥−log⁡ρ.T_{P_{f}}\bigl(E_{\rho}(f)/\rho\bigr)\geq-\log\rho.
Proof.

Set τ=−log⁡ρ\tau=-\log\rho and y⁡(τ)=Eρ​(f)/ρy(\tau)=E_{\rho}(f)/\rho. By the scaling identity in Lemma 4.2, ∑iBEρ​(ρ​|f^​(i)|)=ρ​Pf​(y)\sum_{i}B_{E_{\rho}}(\rho|\widehat{f}(i)|)=\rho P_{f}(y). Since Eρ′=−Aρ′E^{\prime}_{\rho}=-A^{\prime}_{\rho}, Proposition 4.3 yields d​y/d​τ=y+Aρ′​(f)≥y+Pf​(y)dy/d\tau=y+A^{\prime}_{\rho}(f)\geq y+P_{f}(y). Hence dd​τ​TPf​(y⁡(τ))≥1\frac{d}{d\tau}T_{P_{f}}(y(\tau))\geq 1 for τ>0\tau>0. Booleanity and finite dimension give y⁡(τ)→0y(\tau)\to 0 as τ↓0\tau\downarrow 0. The clock is finite and continuous at zero: for 0<y≤10<y\leq 1, Pf​(y)≥Pf​(1)>0P_{f}(y)\geq P_{f}(1)>0. Integrating on [η,τ][\eta,\tau] and taking η↓0\eta\downarrow 0 proves the clock inequality. ∎

More generally, let

The weights cjc_{j} and arguments qjq_{j} are fixed as ρ\rho varies; they may depend on the source cell under consideration. The clock TQT_{Q} is finite at zero and strictly increasing. If Q≤PfQ\leq P_{f}, then TPf≤TQT_{P_{f}}\leq T_{Q}.

4.4. Propagation of an integrated entropy bound

One clock comparison at the left endpoint will cover every larger correlation. The envelope must stay fixed while the correlation varies.

Theorem 4.6 (Propagation to larger correlations).

Let f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} satisfy W1​(f)>0W_{1}(f)>0, and let QQ have the fixed finite-sum form (4.5), with Q≤PfQ\leq P_{f} on (0,∞)(0,\infty). Fix 0<ρ0<10<\rho_{0}<1 and a constant ϵ∈[0,1)\epsilon\in[0,1), and suppose that

TQ​(H⁡(ρ0)/ρ0)≤(1−ϵ)​log⁡(1/ρ0).T_{Q}\bigl(H(\rho_{0})/\rho_{0}\bigr)\leq(1-\epsilon)\log(1/\rho_{0}).

Then, for ρ0≤ρ<1\rho_{0}\leq\rho<1,

TQ​(H⁡(ρ)/ρ)≤(1−ϵ)​log⁡(1/ρ),Eρ​(f)≥H⁡(ρ)​ρ−ϵ.T_{Q}\bigl(H(\rho)/\rho\bigr)\leq(1-\epsilon)\log(1/\rho),\qquad E_{\rho}(f)\geq H(\rho)\rho^{-\epsilon}.

In particular, the choice ϵ=0\epsilon=0 gives Eρ​(f)≥H⁡(ρ)E_{\rho}(f)\geq H(\rho) for ρ0≤ρ≤1\rho_{0}\leq\rho\leq 1.

Here ϵ\epsilon specifies a guaranteed fractional saving relative to the dictator’s clock value log⁡(1/ρ)\log(1/\rho); it remains fixed as ρ\rho varies. The value ϵ=0\epsilon=0 gives the non-strict bound, while ϵ>0\epsilon>0 yields the factor ρ−ϵ>1\rho^{-\epsilon}>1 in the entropy estimate. We first record the monotonicity of the individual profile ratios.

Lemma 4.7.

For 0<a<10<a<1, the function u↦F−1​(F⁡(u)/a)/uu\mapsto F^{-1}(F(u)/a)/u is strictly increasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty). For a=1a=1 it equals one.

Proof.

Put v=F−1​(F⁡(u)/a)v=F^{-1}(F(u)/a), so 0<v<u0<v<u. The function 𝒦\mathcal{K} in (4.3) is strictly increasing by the proof of Lemma 4.2. Implicit differentiation gives d​log⁡v/d​log⁡u=𝒦⁡(u)/𝒦⁡(v)>1d\log v/d\log u=\mathcal{K}(u)/\mathcal{K}(v)>1. Thus v/uv/u increases strictly with uu. ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.6.

Let TdicT_{\rm dic} be the clock of the dictator profile By​(1)B_{y}(1). The substitution y=H⁡(t)/ty=H(t)/t gives dy/[y+By(1)]=−dt/tdy/[y+B_{y}(1)]=-dt/t, and therefore

Tdic​(H⁡(ρ)/ρ)=−log⁡ρ.T_{\rm dic}(H(\rho)/\rho)=-\log\rho.

TQ′​(y)Tdic′​(y)=x⁡(y)+1x⁡(y)+R⁡(y)\frac{T^{\prime}_{Q}(y)}{T^{\prime}_{\rm dic}(y)}=\frac{x(y)+1}{x(y)+R(y)}

is nondecreasing on the initial interval where R≥1R\geq 1. On the remaining interval it is at least one.

This average is nondecreasing while it is below one: first it averages an increasing function, and later all new values are at least one. If the average ever exceeds one, every later average remains strictly above one. The assumed fractional bound at H⁡(ρ0)/ρ0H(\rho_{0})/\rho_{0} therefore holds at every smaller positive yy. Since H⁡(ρ)/ρH(\rho)/\rho decreases with ρ\rho, this proves the first assertion.

The profile-clock theorem and Q≤PfQ\leq P_{f} give TQ​(Eρ​(f)/ρ)≥−log⁡ρT_{Q}(E_{\rho}(f)/\rho)\geq-\log\rho, hence Eρ​(f)≥H⁡(ρ)E_{\rho}(f)\geq H(\rho). Subtracting the clock bound just proved yields

ϵ​log⁡(1/ρ)≤∫H⁡(ρ)/ρEρ​(f)/ρd​yy+Q⁡(y)≤log⁡Eρ​(f)H⁡(ρ).\epsilon\log(1/\rho)\leq\int_{H(\rho)/\rho}^{E_{\rho}(f)/\rho}\frac{dy}{y+Q(y)}\leq\log\frac{E_{\rho}(f)}{H(\rho)}.

4.5. Profiles controlled by one or two coordinates

To use the clock in a finite certificate, we replace the full singleton profile by a lower bound depending on one or two retained coefficients and a lower bound for W1W_{1}. Concavity shows that the remaining squared mass may be concentrated at its allowed cap.

Lemma 4.8.

Let f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} be increasing. Suppose f^​(1)∈[a,A]\widehat{f}(1)\in[a,A], where 0≤a≤A≤10\leq a\leq A\leq 1, and W1≥wW_{1}\geq w. Set c1=min⁡(A,1−a)c_{1}=\min(A,1-a). This redistribution relaxes the Fourier constraints; its concentrated profile need not be realizable by a Boolean source. The resulting bound depends only on the cell parameters.

The same concavity also reduces the number of source values that need checking. Recall that a polytope is the convex hull of finitely many points in Euclidean space. Every point is a convex combination of its vertices, so a convex function on a polytope attains its maximum at a vertex. We apply this observation when the remaining squared masses depend affinely on the retained squared coefficients.

Lemma 4.9 (Convexity in squared influences).

Let KK be a polytope and let ℓ1,…,ℓm:K→[0,∞)\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{m}:K\to[0,\infty) be affine functions with ∑jℓj>0\sum_{j}\ell_{j}>0 on KK. For positive weights c1,…,cmc_{1},\ldots,c_{m}, put Qx​(y)=∑jcj​By​(ℓj​(x))Q_{x}(y)=\sum_{j}c_{j}B_{y}(\sqrt{\ell_{j}(x)}). For every Y>0Y>0, the function

x⟼∫0Yd​yy+Qx​(y)x\longmapsto\int_{0}^{Y}\frac{dy}{y+Q_{x}(y)}

is convex on KK and attains its maximum at a vertex.

Proof.

Lemma 4.2 makes Qx​(y)Q_{x}(y) concave in xx. Since the reciprocal is convex and decreasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty), 1/(y+Qx​(y))1/(y+Q_{x}(y)) is convex in xx. Integration preserves convexity; the integral is finite because Qx​(y)≥Qx​(Y)>0Q_{x}(y)\geq Q_{x}(Y)>0 for 0<y≤Y0<y\leq Y. If x=∑rθr​vrx=\sum_{r}\theta_{r}v_{r} is a convex combination of vertices, convexity bounds the integral at xx by the corresponding weighted average at the vrv_{r}, hence by their largest value. This proves the last assertion. ∎

The next observation allows the cap itself to vary. It removes artificial subdivisions when a source constraint gives an exact cap.

Lemma 4.10 (Concavity with a varying cap).

Let b:[0,∞)→ℝb:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R} be continuous, concave, and twice continuously differentiable on (0,∞)(0,\infty). On an interval II, let c:I→(0,∞)c:I\to(0,\infty) be convex and twice continuously differentiable, and let w:I→ℝw:I\to\mathbb{R} be affine. If k≥0k\geq 0 and 0≤w−k​c≤c0\leq w-kc\leq c on II, then k​b​(c)+b⁡(w−k​c)kb(c)+b(w-kc) is concave.

5. Entropy and energy at intermediate correlations

This section covers 457/500≤ρ≤49/50457/500\leq\rho\leq 49/50. The local bounds from Section 3 handle functions close to one or two coordinates; a fourth-moment estimate pays the mean correction uniformly. For the remaining sources, we split according to the first-level energy W1W_{1}. If it is small, Harris’s inequality controls W2W_{2} and a cubic energy bound proves CK. If it is large, the integrated entropy bound proves the stronger inequality Eρ​(f)≥H⁡(ρ)E_{\rho}(f)\geq H(\rho). The certificate assigns each source cell to one of these arguments and checks that the cells cover every source.

5.1. Conditional Harris inequalities without balance

Harris association bounds W2W_{2} in terms of W1W_{1} and one or two retained coefficients. These are the source constraints needed by the cubic energy bound in the next subsection.

Theorem 5.1 (Harris inequality [13]).

Let X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} be independent signs, with arbitrary individual biases. For increasing functions f,g:{−1,1}n→ℝf,g:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}, Cov⁡(f⁡(X),g⁡(X))≥0\Cov(f(X),g(X))\geq 0.

We apply this theorem to the monotone source obtained by compression. It remains valid after conditioning on any coordinates, because the unconditioned coordinates still have a product law.

Pairing ff with its noisy dual alternates the signs of the Fourier levels. Conditional Harris association turns that alternation into an upper bound on W2W_{2}.

The dual fd​(x)=−f⁡(−x)f^{\rm d}(x)=-f(-x) is increasing and satisfies fd^​(S)=(−1)|S|+1​f^​(S)\widehat{f^{\rm d}}(S)=(-1)^{|S|+1}\widehat{f}(S), including the constant coefficient −μ-\mu. Conditional association of ff and Tη​fdT_{\eta}f^{\rm d} yields

(5.1) ∑S≠∅(−1)|S|+1​η|S|​f^​(S)2≥∑∅≠S⊆K(−1)|S|+1​η|S|​f^​(S)2.\sum_{S\neq\varnothing}(-1)^{|S|+1}\eta^{|S|}\widehat{f}(S)^{2}\geq\sum_{\varnothing\neq S\subseteq K}(-1)^{|S|+1}\eta^{|S|}\widehat{f}(S)^{2}.

Indeed, the difference is the mean of their conditional covariances outside KK. The global covariance and that of the conditional means both remove the constant term −μ2-\mu^{2}.

Proposition 5.2.

Let f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} be increasing. For 0<η≤10<\eta\leq 1, we have

7. Coordinate projections and the spectral bound

We prove the uniform spectral criterion that handles every source below the local cutoff. Retain the coordinates above a threshold and charge the discarded coordinates to the same profile budget. We first bound the variance of the retained source and the energy of the discarded arcsine field. Combining these bounds gives the scalar criterion in Theorem 7.6.

Throughout this section, write ρ=tanh⁡u\rho=\tanh u, g=Tρ​fg=T_{\rho}f, and h=arcsin⁡gh=\arcsin g. We retain the entropy correction 𝒥\mathcal{J} from (6.1) and the profile height ℓu\ell_{u} from (6.5). For K⊆[n]K\subseteq[n], define

(7.1) PK​h=𝔼⁡[h∣XK].P_{K}h=\mathbb{E}[h\mid X_{K}].

This averages over the coordinates outside KK and is the orthogonal projection onto functions of XKX_{K}. In Fourier language it keeps exactly the terms with S⊆KS\subseteq K; the remainder h−PK​hh-P_{K}h contains every term using an outside coordinate. This decomposition allows separate estimates for dependence carried by the retained coordinates and for the energy needed to support the remainder. Throughout this section, f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\} is nonconstant and increasing. We retain the full budget D⁡(g)/ρD(g)/\rho from Proposition 6.2. This gives a direct lower bound for entropy production at every positive gap.

7.1. An influence bound for bounded functions

Conditional sources take values in [−1,1][-1,1]. The following theorem bounds their variance by an explicit cost for each influence, without assuming monotonicity.

We express the variance bound in terms of the function

(7.2) ψ⁡(a)=min⁡{a+a22,2​a​(1−a/4)log⁡(4/a)}(0<a≤1),ψ⁡(0)=0.\psi(a)=\min\left\{\frac{a+a^{2}}{2},\frac{2a(1-a/4)}{\log(4/a)}\right\}\quad(0<a\leq 1),\qquad\psi(0)=0.
Theorem 7.1 (Variance and influences).

For every g:{−1,1}n→[−1,1]g:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to[-1,1] and every K⊆[n]K\subseteq[n],

Var⁡(PK​g)≤∑i∈Kψ⁡(‖∂ig‖1).\Var(P_{K}g)\leq\sum_{i\in K}\psi(\|\partial_{i}g\|_{1}).

In particular, Var⁡(g)≤∑iψ⁡(‖∂ig‖1)\Var(g)\leq\sum_{i}\psi(\|\partial_{i}g\|_{1}).

The estimate is a quantitative form of the following influence inequality.

Theorem 7.2 (Talagrand’s influence inequality [25, 7]).

There is a universal constant C>0C>0 such that, for every f:{−1,1}n→ℝf:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R},

Var⁡(f)≤C​∑i=1n‖∂if‖221+log⁡(‖∂if‖2/‖∂if‖1).\Var(f)\leq C\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\|\partial_{i}f\|_{2}^{2}}{1+\log(\|\partial_{i}f\|_{2}/\|\partial_{i}f\|_{1})}.

We now prove the explicit bounded-function estimate used here.

Fourier expansion gives Var⁡(g)=∑i∫01‖Ts​∂ig‖22​𝑑s\Var(g)=\sum_{i}\int_{0}^{1}\|T_{\sqrt{s}}\partial_{i}g\|_{2}^{2}\,ds. Indeed, a mode of degree jj contributes sj−1s^{j-1} in each of its jj coordinates. Fix ii and write a=‖∂ig‖1a=\|\partial_{i}g\|_{1}. Since |∂ig|≤1|\partial_{i}g|\leq 1, the integrand is at most (1−s)​a2+s​a(1-s)a^{2}+sa by its Fourier expansion, and at most a2/(1+s)a^{2/(1+s)} by hypercontractivity. For monotone gg, ∂ig≥0\partial_{i}g\geq 0, so ‖∂ig‖1=g^​(i)\|\partial_{i}g\|_{1}=\widehat{g}(i). This is the form used for the Boolean source below.

7.2. Retaining the pivot energy in a martingale decomposition

We next bound the energy of the part discarded by projection, using the martingale entropy argument of Falik and Samorodnitsky [9, Theorem 2.2 and Lemma 2.3]. Reveal the coordinates one at a time and subtract successive conditional expectations. These differences are the Doob martingale increments: each records the additional dependence revealed at that step. Its Fourier terms all contain the newly revealed coordinate, so it already contributes one unit of degree before the other coordinates are counted. Keeping that contribution strengthens the log-Sobolev estimate used below.

Let h:{−1,1}n→ℝh:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} and K⊆[n]K\subseteq[n]. Set

V=‖h−PK​h‖22​and ​bK=∑i∉K(𝔼​|∂ih|)2.V=\|h-P_{K}h\|_{2}^{2}\enskip\text{and }b_{K}=\sum_{i\notin K}(\mathbb{E}|\partial_{i}h|)^{2}.

Dir⁡(h−PK​h)≥(1+λ2)​V−eλ−12​bK.\operatorname{Dir}(h-P_{K}h)\geq\left(1+\frac{\lambda}{2}\right)V-\frac{e^{\lambda-1}}{2}b_{K}.

Order the coordinates of KK before its complement, and let hi:{−1,1}n→ℝh_{i}:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} be the Doob increments of hh in this order, so hi=𝔼[h∣X1,…,Xi]−𝔼[h∣X1,…,Xi−1]h_{i}=\mathbb{E}[h\mid X_{1},\ldots,X_{i}]-\mathbb{E}[h\mid X_{1},\ldots,X_{i-1}]. The log-Sobolev part of Theorem 3.1, applied to gig_{i}, gives Ent⁡(hi2)≤2​[Dir⁡(hi)−‖hi‖22]\Ent(h_{i}^{2})\leq 2[\operatorname{Dir}(h_{i})-\|h_{i}\|_{2}^{2}]. 8. Completion of the qualitative proof

The same uniform spectral bound can reach the local entropy region even as that region shrinks toward a dictator. We first state the local threshold, then choose spectral parameters whose losses remain small enough to meet it. Together these estimates complete the proof of CK.

Also u−v≤7​h/4u-v\leq 7h/4 and u≥8u\geq 8 imply

1−uv​(a0+ρ2​d/2)≥54​h,4​uv​(1+4​h+3​h2)<10125.1-\frac{u}{v}(a_{0}+\rho^{2}d/2)\geq\frac{5}{4}h,\qquad\frac{4u}{v}(1+4h+3h^{2})<\frac{101}{25}.

Writing 𝒬¯u​(a0)\overline{\mathcal{Q}}_{u}(a_{0}) for the upper cost and using u/v≥1u/v\geq 1 in the arcsine saving now gives

N−u​𝒬¯u​(a0)h\displaystyle\frac{N-u\overline{\mathcal{Q}}_{u}(a_{0})}{h} >3​(u2+910)−10110−37​(2​u+1)+4\displaystyle>3\left(\frac{u}{2}+\frac{9}{10}\right)-\frac{101}{10}-\frac{3}{7}(2u+1)+4

The four terms record the spectral gain, degree-correction cost, entropy penalty, and arcsine saving, respectively; their sum is a positive linear function of uu. All costs are therefore below N/uN/u, proving the derivative assertion by Theorem 7.6. ∎

8.3. Completion of the proof

The compact spectral calculation uses the same moving local cutoff throughout. It consequently gives a derivative criterion for every possible positive-gap source without a separate neighborhood theorem.

Proposition 8.3.

For every increasing f:{−1,1}n→{−1,1}f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}, if 49/50≤ρ≤tanh⁡849/50\leq\rho\leq\tanh 8 and Gf​(ρ)>0G_{f}(\rho)>0, then Gf′​(ρ)>0G_{f}^{\prime}(\rho)>0.

Computer-assisted proof.

Lemma 3.6 rules out positive gap when α≥1−2​e−u\alpha\geq 1-2e^{-u}. For the remaining sources, Theorem 7.6 gives D⁡(Tρ​f)>ρ​uD(T_{\rho}f)>\rho u, hence Gf′​(ρ)>0G_{f}^{\prime}(\rho)>0. The certificate verifies this criterion on 24 closed noise intervals covering [45951/20000,8][45951/20000,8], always with the cutoff 1−2​e−u1-2e^{-u}. Since log⁡9<45951/20000<atanh⁡(49/50)\log 9<45951/20000<\atanh(49/50), both the local cutoff and the spectral cover apply throughout the stated range. Appendix A gives the verification details. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Proposition 3.15 gives 0≤ρ≤457/5000\leq\rho\leq 457/500; Theorems 5.6 and 5.7 give 457/500≤ρ≤49/50457/500\leq\rho\leq 49/50. Fix an increasing nonconstant source. We claim that every positive-gap point with 49/50≤ρ<149/50\leq\rho<1 has Gf′​(ρ)>0G_{f}^{\prime}(\rho)>0. Proposition 8.3 proves this through u=8u=8. For u≥8u\geq 8, Lemma 8.1 excludes positive gap when δ⁡(f)≤(3/2)​e−u\delta(f)\leq(3/2)e^{-u}; the dictator case is exact. Proposition 8.2 covers every remaining source. The claim follows.

Since Gf​(1)=−Φ⁡(μ)≤0G_{f}(1)=-\Phi(\mu)\leq 0, the differential barrier in Lemma 2.2 now proves CK throughout [49/50,1][49/50,1]. Compress an arbitrary source at the fixed correlation in question; constants have zero information. All intervals are closed, and the endpoint assertions are 0≤00\leq 0 and H⁡(μ)≤log⁡2H(\mu)\leq\log 2. ∎

Appendix A Certificates and reproducibility

Fixed low-correlation signs are checked by rational series bounds; the other transcendental signs are checked on complete closed rational domains by outward-rounded Arb arithmetic [15]. The moving-cap source boundaries are quadratic algebraic numbers reconstructed exactly. A strict sign is accepted only when the entire enclosure has that sign; a nonfinite enclosure or one containing zero is inconclusive. Exact rational and algebraic arithmetic checks coverage. Every supporting line is valid by convexity; its explicit integral is accepted only after the required denominator and final signs pass. The compact inverse profile is bounded analytically. Bisections retain both children unless infeasibility is proved. Data-free scripts check the finite constants in the analytic argument of Proposition 8.2 and the local junction in Lemma 8.1.

A.1. The compact certificate

The qualitative file qualitative_compact_certificate.json covers [45951/20000,8][45951/20000,8] by 24 closed rational noise intervals: eight equal intervals through 44, followed by 16 intervals of length 1/41/4. The cutoff is 1−2​e−u1-2e^{-u} throughout, and Lemma 3.6 covers every larger influence. The single explicit parameter rule uses 96 height endpoint inequalities from Lemma 7.7. No height records or fitted parameter families are stored. The split is 2​u/32u/3, and Lemma 7.8 supplies the upper endpoint without root calculations. Exact adjacency checks verify the noise partition.

The replay qualitative_compact_verify.py recomputes every scalar sign at 256 bits. It clears positive denominators and expands logarithms of profile ratios before interval evaluation, retaining cancellation without changing the signs. The transfer condition is proved analytically. The separate qualitative_compact_audit.py uses independently derived unscaled formulas, 384-bit arithmetic, and first-order bounds on the full extended height domain. Both verify the full stated domain and its moving influence cutoff. Neither uses an optimizer or inverse roots.

A.2. Files and replay scope

The certificate data and verification code are available in the GitHub repository linked below. The low-correlation argument uses ten fixed endpoint inequalities and no correlation partition. The middle-range checks use ten scalar endpoint gates, five local endpoint signs, and 29 clocks with 56 integration intervals and 152 supporting-line evaluations. The two-coordinate mean bound uses eight fixed rational signs and no mean partition. The unbounded endpoint argument is analytic; its checker verifies the finite constants used in that argument, without sampling the unbounded domain.

From the bundle root, install requirements.txt and run python3 verify.py. This checks the file manifest and runs the ten numerical stages supporting the exact theorem. Each stage recomputes its signs and domain coverage and writes its report to a fresh output directory. Optimized Python is rejected because the verifiers use assertions. The separate stability paper has its own package and stronger quantitative checks; none of them is an input to this exact proof. The README.md records the build and replay commands. Only current inputs are included. The certificate data and verification code are available at https://github.com/vukhacky/courtade-kumar-conjecture/.
